Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned A.G.A. for the respondents.

2. The relief sought in this petition is for quashing of the F.I.R. dated 27.8.2023 registered as Case Crime No. 704 of 2023, under Sections 506, 471, 468, 406 and 420 I.P.C., P.S. Kotwali Orai,
District-Jalaun.
Further prayer has been made not to arrest the petitioner in the aforesaid case.

sentences.text: 3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that petitioner has no complicity in the instant case.
The whole prosecution story is totally false and frivolous and the petitioner has been falsely implicated with ulterior motive and mala-fide intention.

4. Learned A.G.A. has vehemently opposed the writ petition and submits that the petitioner is a habitual offender and even previously he has challenged another First Information Report by filing Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 877 of 2024, which was registered as Case Crime No. 393 of 2023,
under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 506 and 120B I.P.C., P.S. Sipri Bazar, District-Jhansi before before this Court, which was dismissed vide order dated 8.2.2024, as cognizable offence was made out against the petitioner.

entities.text: Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 877 of 2024
entities.label: CASE_NUMBER

sentences.text:
Then another writ petition was instituted by co-accused in which the petitioner was also an accused, challenging the F.I.R. dated 27.8.2023, under sections 420, 406,
467, 468, 471 and 506 I.P.C., P.S. Kotwali Orai, District-Jalaun and the same was also dismissed by co-ordinate Bench of this Court, vide order dated 13.10.2023.

Now he has placed another F.I.R.
dated 10.11.2023, which was registered as Case Crime No. 400 of 2023, wherein the petitioner is also a named accused.

5. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India : (2007) 8 SCC 449 held that in exercising power under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the High Court is not just a court of law, but is also a court of equity and a person who invokes the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, is duty bound to place all the facts before the Court without any reservation.

entities.text: Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India : (2007) 8 SCC 449
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If there is suppression of material facts or twisted facts have been placed before the High Court then it will be fully justified in refusing to entertain petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

6. The Apex Court Court while referring to the judgment of Scrutton, LJ. in R v. Kensington Income Tax Commissioners, observed as under:-
"In exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court will always keep in mind the conduct of the party who is invoking such jurisdiction.

entities.text: R v. Kensington Income Tax Commissioners
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the applicant does not disclose full facts or suppresses relevant materials or is otherwise-guilty of misleading the Court, then the Court may dismiss the action without adjudicating the matter on merits.
The rule has been evolved in larger public interest to deter unscrupulous litigants from abusing the process of Court by deceiving it.

The very basis of the writ jurisdiction rests in disclosure of true,
complete and correct facts.

If the material facts are not candidly stated or are suppressed or are distorted, the very functioning of the writ courts would become impossible."
7.

In Welcome Hotel and Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors. etc. AIR 1983 SC 1015, the Apex Court has held that a party which has misled the Court in passing an order in its favour is not entitled to be heard on the merits of the case.

entities.text: Welcome Hotel and Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors. etc. AIR 1983 SC 1015
entities.label: PRECEDENT

8. In Ram Preeti Yadav Vs. U.P. Board of High School and Intermediate Education and others, 2003 (Suppl.) 3 SCR 352, it was reiterated after referring to various earlier decisions of the Apex Court Bhanu Pratap Shakya vs State Of Up And 2 Others on 12 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182350477/

9. In R. Vishwanatha Pillai Vs. State of Kerala & others, JT 2004(1) SC 88 the Apex Court observed that a person, who seeks equity, must act in a fair and equitable manner.

entities.text: R. Vishwanatha Pillai Vs. State of Kerala & others, JT 2004(1) SC 88
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 10. In State of Andhra Pradesh & another Vs. T. Suryachandra Rao, AIR 2005 SC 3110, the Apex Court after referring to various earlier decisions held that suppression of a material document would also amount to a fraud on the Court.

entities.text: State of Andhra Pradesh & another Vs. T. Suryachandra Rao, AIR 2005 SC 3110

The same view has been reiterated in Bhaurao Dagdu Paralkar Vs. State of Maharashtra & others, AIR 2005 SC 3330.
11.

entities.text: Bhaurao Dagdu Paralkar Vs. State of Maharashtra & others, AIR 2005 SC 3330
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. and Ors., [2008 (12) SCC 481] the Apex Court has held that the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 and of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution is extraordinary, equitable and discretionary and it is imperative that the petitioner approaching the Writ Court must come with clean hands and put forward all the facts before the Court without concealing or suppressing anything and seek an appropriate relief.

entities.text: K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. and Ors., [2008 (12) SCC 481]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If there is no candid disclosure of relevant and material facts or the petitioner is guilty of misleading the Court, his petition may be dismissed at the threshold without considering the merits of the claim.

The same rule was reiterated in G. Jayshree and Ors. v. Bhagwandas S. Patel and Ors.: (2009) 3 SCC 141.
12. In Dalip Singh Versus State of Uttar Pradesh and others [(2010) 2 Supreme Court Cases 114], the Apex Court seriously criticized the making of false statement on oath and the attempt of a litigant in misleading the Court.
13.

entities.text: G. Jayshree and Ors. v. Bhagwandas S. Patel and Ors.: (2009) 3 SCC 141
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Dalip Singh Versus State of Uttar Pradesh and others [(2010) 2 Supreme Court Cases 114]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is settled law that one should approach the Court with clean heart and clean mind to get a relief and one who does not come with clean heart and clean mind, dis-entitles himself from getting any relief from the Court.
From what has been mentioned above, it is clear that the petitioner has filed this writ petition with oblique motives and has not presented the correct facts just to gain undue advantage.
Such type of practice should always be discouraged and is highly deprecated.
They belong to the category of persons who not only attempt, but succeed in polluting the course of justice.
14. Thus, keeping in view the above catena of judgements, we are of the considered opinion that the present writ petition is liable to be dismissed on the ground of concealment of facts.

15. Though the case has been set up but does not inspire us to entertain the writ petition instead of dismissing the writ petition with heavy costs as the counsel has concealed the correct facts but keeping in mind that learned counsel is a young Advocate who prays for that the writ petition may be dismissed as not pressed, at this stage.
17. In view of the above, the writ petition is dismissed as not pressed with the observation that the dismissal of this petition will not cause any prejudice to the interest of petitioner.
18. Needless to say, it is always open for the petitioner to invoke the remedy as available in law.
